professor.name: Dr. Gomez
professor.text: Many universities now record lectures and post them online. Some educators think this helps students learn because they can review difficult material at their own pace. Others worry that students stop attending class and lose the benefits of live discussion. What do you think? Should universities record all lectures and make them available online? Why or why not?

students.name: Kelly
students.text: I think recordings are very useful. When a professor speaks quickly, I can pause the video and take better notes. Students who are sick or who work part-time also don't fall behind.

students.name: Andrew
students.text: I disagree. If every lecture is online, many students will just stay home, and class discussions will become empty. Asking questions in person is an important part of learning.

professor.name: Professor Tan
professor.text: Cities around the world are trying to reduce traffic in their downtown areas. One approach is to make public transportation completely free. Supporters say this would encourage people to leave their cars at home. Critics argue that the money would be better spent improving service. If you were advising a city government, would you recommend free public transportation? Explain your view.

students.name: Maria
students.text: Free transportation is a great idea. Many people drive because bus tickets add up over a month. If buses were free, more people would try them, and there would be less pollution.

students.name: Jason
students.text: I'm not convinced. Price isn't the main problem where I live—the buses are slow and come only every half hour. A free bus that never arrives on time won't change anyone's habits.

professor.name: Dr. Williams
professor.text: Some companies have started offering employees a four-day work week with the same pay, as long as the work gets done. Supporters say workers become happier and more productive. Others believe it is unrealistic for many types of businesses. Do you think a four-day work week is a good idea for most companies? Why or why not?

students.name: Priya
students.text: I think it could work well. People who have more rest are more focused, so they might get the same amount done in four days. It would also help companies attract good workers.

students.name: Tom
students.text: It sounds nice, but it doesn't fit every job. Hospitals, stores, and restaurants need staff every day. Those businesses would have to hire more people, which could be very expensive.

professor.name: Professor Ahmed
professor.text: This week we are discussing how people form habits. Some researchers recommend changing one small habit at a time, while others suggest that big life changes, such as moving to a new city, are the best moment to change many habits at once. Which approach do you think is more effective for building good habits, and why?

students.name: Lucas
students.text: Small changes are more realistic. When I tried to change everything at once in January, I gave up after a week. Starting with one habit, like going to bed earlier, is easier to keep.

students.name: Hannah
students.text: I think big changes can actually help. When I moved to college, I had no old routine, so it was easy to start exercising and cooking. A new environment gives you a fresh start.

professor.name: Dr. Okafor
professor.text: Many supermarkets now charge customers a small fee for plastic bags. The goal is to reduce plastic waste, but some people say the fee is unfair to low-income shoppers or simply moves the problem elsewhere. In your opinion, is charging for plastic bags an effective way to protect the environment? Explain why.

students.name: Sofia
students.text: Yes, I think it works. In my town, people started bringing their own bags almost immediately after the fee was introduced. Even a small cost makes people think about their choices.

students.name: Daniel
students.text: I'm doubtful. Many people now buy plastic trash bags instead of reusing shopping bags, so the total amount of plastic may not change much. We need bigger solutions.

professor.name: Professor Hill
professor.text: Volunteering is often seen as an important part of being a good citizen. Some high schools now require students to complete a certain number of volunteer hours before they can graduate. Do you think schools should make volunteering a graduation requirement? Why or why not?

students.name: Emma
students.text: I support the requirement. Many teenagers never think about volunteering until someone asks them to. Once they try it, they often discover causes they care about.

students.name: Ryan
students.text: Forcing people to volunteer goes against the whole idea. Students will just do the minimum to get the hours, and organizations may end up with helpers who don't want to be there.

professor.name: Dr. Russo
professor.text: More and more people get their news from short videos on social media rather than from newspapers or television. Some say this makes news more accessible, especially for young people. Others worry that short videos cannot explain complex issues properly. What is your view? Is getting news from short videos a positive or negative trend?

students.name: Aiko
students.text: I see it as positive. Many of my friends never read newspapers, but they watch short news videos every day. At least they know what is happening in the world.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: The problem is that a one-minute video can't give context. People see a dramatic clip and form strong opinions without understanding the full story. That can make debates more extreme.

professor.name: Professor Lindqvist
professor.text: Governments sometimes provide financial support to industries they consider strategically important, such as renewable energy or computer chip manufacturing. Proponents argue that early support helps new industries become competitive. Critics contend that governments are poor at choosing winners and that subsidies distort markets. Should governments subsidize specific industries? Use reasons and examples to support your position.

students.name: Fatima
students.text: I think targeted support is justified when the benefits extend beyond a single company. Solar power became affordable partly because early subsidies allowed producers to scale up, and now the whole economy benefits from cheaper energy.

students.name: Oliver
students.text: Subsidies often end up protecting inefficient firms long after they should have adapted. Once an industry receives money, it lobbies to keep it. I'd prefer governments to fund basic research and let companies compete.

professor.name: Dr. Haddad
professor.text: Artificial intelligence tools can now write essays, summarize readings, and solve problems. Some instructors want to ban these tools in coursework, while others believe students should learn to use them responsibly as they will in the workplace. How do you think universities should respond to AI tools in student assignments? Explain your reasoning.

students.name: Grace
students.text: Banning them is unrealistic and probably impossible to enforce. Universities should redesign assignments so that students have to show their own reasoning, for example through drafts or oral explanations, while still allowing AI for brainstorming.

students.name: Victor
students.text: I think some courses should ban them, at least at the beginning. If students rely on AI before they've developed basic writing skills, they'll never learn to structure an argument themselves.

professor.name: Professor Lin
professor.text: Some cities have introduced taxes on sugary drinks to reduce health problems such as obesity and diabetes. Evidence suggests that consumption falls after such taxes are introduced, but critics say the taxes place a heavier burden on low-income families and limit personal choice. Do you think taxes on sugary drinks are a good public health policy? Why or why not?

students.name: Noah
students.text: The evidence is persuasive. If purchases drop and the revenue is spent on health programs or free drinking water in schools, low-income communities actually benefit the most.

students.name: Isabella
students.text: I'm uncomfortable with policies that change behavior by making daily life more expensive for people with the least money. Education and better access to healthy food would address the causes rather than punishing the symptoms.

professor.name: Dr. Moreau
professor.text: When historic buildings are no longer used for their original purpose, cities must decide what to do with them. Some argue that these buildings should be carefully preserved as they are, while others believe they should be adapted for new uses, even if this means significant changes to their interiors. Which approach do you favor, and why?

students.name: Elena
students.text: Adaptation keeps buildings alive. An old factory turned into apartments or a library is used every day, and the community stays connected to its history in a practical way.

students.name: James
students.text: Some changes destroy exactly what made a building valuable. Once original interiors are removed, they can't be restored. I think at least the most significant buildings should be protected from major alterations.

professor.name: Professor Diaz
professor.text: Many minority languages around the world are losing speakers as younger generations shift to more widely used languages. Some people believe that governments should invest heavily in preserving these languages through schools and media. Others argue that language change is natural and that resources should go elsewhere. What is your position on this issue?

students.name: Amara
students.text: A language carries knowledge, stories, and ways of seeing the world that can't be fully translated. When it disappears, that knowledge is lost for everyone, so public investment is worth it.

students.name: Ethan
students.text: Preservation programs often fail if families themselves don't see a benefit in using the language. Rather than large government programs, support should go to communities that actively want to keep their language.

professor.name: Dr. Carter
professor.text: Some companies publish the salaries of all their employees so that everyone can see what others earn. Supporters say this transparency reduces unfair pay gaps. Opponents worry that it creates conflict and invades employees' privacy. Should companies make all salaries public within the organization? Explain your view with reasons and examples.

students.name: Mei
students.text: Transparency forces companies to justify their decisions. Pay gaps between men and women, for example, are much harder to maintain when everyone can see the numbers.

students.name: Liam
students.text: Salaries depend on many factors that aren't visible, such as negotiation or special skills. Publishing them could lead to resentment and make employees feel judged by colleagues.

professor.name: Professor Brown
professor.text: Some schools give students a lot of homework every day. Other schools give very little homework so that students have time for sports, hobbies, and family. Which do you think is better for students: more homework or less homework? Why?

students.name: Mia
students.text: I think more homework is better. Practicing at home helps students remember what they learned in class, and it prepares them for exams.

students.name: Leo
students.text: I prefer less homework. Students are already tired after school. They need time to relax, play sports, and spend time with their families.

professor.name: Dr. Silva
professor.text: Many people use their phones right before they go to sleep. Some experts say this is bad for sleep, but others think it is a good way to relax. Should people stop using their phones one hour before bed? Why or why not?

students.name: Chloe
students.text: Yes, I think so. When I read on my phone at night, I fall asleep much later. Reading a paper book helps me sleep better.

students.name: Sam
students.text: I don't agree. Listening to music or watching a short video on my phone helps me relax after a busy day. It depends on what you do with the phone.

professor.name: Professor Kim
professor.text: Some people like to live in big cities, while others prefer small towns. Each place has advantages. If you could choose, would you prefer to live in a big city or a small town? Explain why.

students.name: Olivia
students.text: I would choose a big city. There are more jobs, museums, and restaurants, and public transportation makes it easy to go everywhere.

students.name: Ben
students.text: I prefer small towns. They are quieter and safer, and people know their neighbors. Life is less stressful when everything is close.

professor.name: Dr. Evans
professor.text: Many students have part-time jobs while they are studying at university. Some people think this is a good experience. Others think students should focus only on their studies. Is it a good idea for university students to have part-time jobs? Why or why not?

students.name: Zoe
students.text: Yes, it is a good idea. Students learn to manage money and time, and they get experience that helps them find a job after graduation.

students.name: Adam
students.text: I think students should focus on studying. A job takes a lot of time and energy, and grades can become worse.

professor.name: Professor Reyes
professor.text: Online shopping has become extremely popular, and many small local stores have closed as a result. Some people say this is simply progress and that customers benefit from lower prices and more choice. Others think communities lose something important when local shops disappear. What is your opinion? Should people make an effort to shop at local stores?

students.name: Nina
students.text: I try to shop locally when I can. Local stores create jobs in the neighborhood and make streets more lively. Saving a few dollars online isn't worth losing that.

students.name: Chris
students.text: Most people simply can't afford to pay more. Online shopping saves time and money, especially for busy families. Stores need to adapt instead of expecting customers to support them.

professor.name: Dr. Park
professor.text: Some universities require all first-year students to take courses outside their major, such as art, history, or science. Supporters say this gives students a broader education. Others think students should be free to focus on their chosen field from the start. Should universities require students to take courses outside their major? Why or why not?

students.name: Rachel
students.text: Yes. I took a philosophy course I didn't want to take, and it completely changed the way I think about my engineering projects. You can't know what's useful until you try it.

students.name: Kevin
students.text: University is expensive, and students should be able to spend their time and money on what they actually need for their careers. Required courses can feel like a waste.

professor.name: Dr. Brown
professor.text: Many students skip breakfast because they are in a hurry or do not have enough money. Some universities now offer free breakfast in the morning. Supporters say that students learn better when they are not hungry. Others say that the money should be used for other services. Do you think universities should offer free breakfast? Why or why not?

students.name: Lily
students.text: I think free breakfast is a good idea. I often skip breakfast, and then I feel tired in my first class. A simple meal in the morning would help many students.

students.name: Omar
students.text: I disagree. Most students can buy their own breakfast, and the university has many other costs. I would rather see that money used for better libraries or study rooms.

professor.name: Professor Green
professor.text: Some students take notes by hand in class, while others use laptops. People who like laptops say that typing is faster and easier to organize. People who like paper say that writing by hand helps them remember more. Which method do you prefer for taking notes in class, and why?

students.name: Nina
students.text: I prefer laptops because I can type much faster than I can write. I also never lose my notes, and I can search them later when I study for an exam.

students.name: Carlos
students.text: I like paper better. When I write by hand, I listen more carefully and think about what is important. A laptop also makes it easy to open social media by mistake.

professor.name: Dr. Reyes
professor.text: Some universities want to make their campuses car-free. Cars would be allowed only at the edge of campus, and everyone would walk, ride bicycles, or use buses inside. Supporters say this would make campus cleaner and safer. Critics say that it would be difficult for some people. What is your opinion about car-free campuses?

students.name: Hannah
students.text: I like the idea. Without cars, the air is cleaner and there is less noise. It would also be safer for students who walk or ride bicycles between classes.

students.name: Ben
students.text: I am not sure. Some students live far away, and others have health problems. A car-free campus might be nice, but it could make life harder for these people.

professor.name: Professor Moore
professor.text: When students go to university, they can live with roommates or live alone. Living with other people can be cheaper and more social. Living alone can be quieter and more private. If you could choose, would you prefer to live with a roommate or alone? Explain your reasons.

students.name: Sara
students.text: I would choose a roommate. It costs less money, and it is nice to have someone to talk to after a hard day. I also feel less lonely in a new city.

students.name: Tom
students.text: I would live alone. I need a quiet place to study, and I like to keep my room in my own way. With a roommate, there is always some noise or a small problem.

professor.name: Dr. Wilson
professor.text: At many universities, the first class of the day starts at eight o'clock in the morning. Some experts say that young adults learn better when classes begin later, for example at ten. Others say that early classes help students plan their day. Should universities start classes later in the morning? Why?

students.name: Ella
students.text: Yes, I think classes should start later. Many students go to bed late because they study or work in the evening, so they are very tired at eight o'clock.

students.name: Jack
students.text: I do not agree. If classes begin later, they also end later, and then students have less free time in the evening. I prefer to finish early and have the whole afternoon.

professor.name: Professor Adams
professor.text: Plastic bottles create a lot of waste on campuses. Some universities have decided to stop selling bottled water and to put water fountains in every building. Supporters say this protects the environment. Critics say that it makes life less convenient. What do you think about this idea?

students.name: Mia
students.text: I support it. Plastic bottles are used for a few minutes and then thrown away. If students carry their own bottles, we would produce much less waste.

students.name: Leo
students.text: I think it is too strict. Sometimes I forget my bottle, and the fountains are not always near my classroom. People should have a choice and be able to buy water when they need it.

professor.name: Dr. Kim
professor.text: Many students study abroad for one semester or one year. They live in a different country and attend classes there. Some people say this is the best way to learn about the world. Others say it is too expensive and not necessary. Do you think studying abroad is worth it?

students.name: Zoe
students.text: Yes, I think it is worth it. Students learn a new language, meet people from other countries, and become more independent. These experiences are useful for a future job.

students.name: Adam
students.text: I think it depends. Studying abroad costs a lot of money, and some students find it too difficult to be far from their families. You can learn about other cultures at home with the internet.

professor.name: Professor Lee
professor.text: Some universities require all students to take a physical education class, such as swimming, running, or yoga. They believe that exercise is important for health and for good grades. Other people say that students should choose their own activities. Should physical education be required for all students?

students.name: Grace
students.text: I think it should be required. Many students spend all day sitting and studying, and they do not exercise. A class would make them move and feel more energetic.

students.name: Noah
students.text: I disagree. Some students already play sports or go to the gym on their own. They should not have to waste time on a class that they do not need.

professor.name: Dr. Ellis
professor.text: A number of companies are experimenting with a four-day work week, in which employees work the same number of hours in four longer days or are paid the same for fewer hours. Supporters believe it makes workers happier and more productive. Critics worry that it could harm customer service. Do you think a four-day work week is a good idea? Explain your reasoning.

students.name: Rachel
students.text: I think it's a good idea. Employees with an extra day off can rest and take care of personal matters, so they return to work with more energy. Several trials have even shown higher productivity.

students.name: Daniel
students.text: I'm not convinced. Many jobs, such as hospitals and shops, need people every day. If everyone works fewer days, someone has to cover the gaps, and that may cost more.

professor.name: Professor Singh
professor.text: Researchers have found that people who take short breaks while studying often remember more than people who study for hours without stopping. However, many students feel that breaks interrupt their concentration and make the work take longer. What is your experience? Do you think taking regular breaks is an effective way to study?

students.name: Isabel
students.text: Breaks work well for me. After about forty minutes my attention drops, so a short walk helps me start again with a clear mind. I get more done in the end.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: I prefer to keep going until I finish a task. When I stop, it takes a long time to get back into the topic, and I often lose my train of thought.

professor.name: Dr. Foster
professor.text: In many courses, a group project receives one grade that every member shares. Teachers say this encourages cooperation. But some students complain that it is unfair when some members work harder than others. Should every student in a group receive the same grade, or should each person be graded individually? Give reasons for your answer.

students.name: Priya
students.text: I think individual grades are fairer. In my last project, two people did almost everything, and the others still received the same mark. That does not reward effort.

students.name: Luke
students.text: I'd keep one shared grade. Teamwork means the group succeeds or fails together, and it pushes members to help each other instead of competing.

professor.name: Professor Rossi
professor.text: Since the pandemic, many companies allow employees to work from home. Some experts predict that this will change our cities, because fewer people will commute to city centers. Others think offices will always be necessary. In your opinion, will remote work have a mostly positive or a mostly negative effect on cities?

students.name: Hana
students.text: I expect mostly positive effects. Less commuting means less traffic and pollution, and people can live in cheaper, quieter areas instead of crowded centers.

students.name: Victor
students.text: I see a risk. If fewer people go downtown, cafés, shops, and public transport will lose customers. City centers might become empty and lose their special energy.

professor.name: Dr. Martin
professor.text: Many museums charge an entrance fee, and these fees help pay for exhibitions and staff. However, some people argue that museums belong to everyone and should be free. Others say that visitors value an experience more when they pay for it. Should public museums be free for all visitors? Why or why not?

students.name: Amara
students.text: They should be free. Culture should not depend on how much money you have, and free entrance would bring in young people and families who might not visit otherwise.

students.name: Tyler
students.text: I disagree. Museums need stable income to protect their collections. A small fee, with discounts for students, is a fair way to keep them open.

professor.name: Professor Nakamura
professor.text: Self-driving cars are being tested in several countries. Their supporters say they will reduce accidents because computers do not get tired or distracted. Critics point out that the technology is not perfect and raises difficult questions about responsibility when something goes wrong. Would you feel comfortable traveling in a self-driving car? Explain your view.

students.name: Elena
students.text: Yes, I would. Most accidents are caused by human mistakes, so a well-tested system could actually be safer than a driver who is sleepy or checking a phone.

students.name: Samir
students.text: Not yet. If the software fails or the sensors don't work in bad weather, nobody can react quickly. I would wait until the technology has a longer record.

professor.name: Dr. Okoye
professor.text: Many universities use standardized test scores, such as national entrance exams, to decide who will be admitted. Supporters say that tests are an objective way to compare students. Critics say that test results measure only a narrow range of skills and may favor students who can afford extra preparation. Should universities rely mainly on standardized tests? Why?

students.name: Julia
students.text: Tests give every applicant the same questions, so they are fairer than opinions or personal connections. Without them, it would be difficult to compare students from different schools.

students.name: Kenji
students.text: I think tests alone are not enough. A student who is creative or hardworking might do poorly on one exam. Interviews and projects show more about a person.

professor.name: Professor Davies
professor.text: In modern workplaces, employees can talk to each other through instant messages, emails, phone calls, and video meetings. Some managers feel that too many messages interrupt people's work, and they suggest more direct conversations. Others like the speed of written messages. Which form of communication do you think works best in a workplace?

students.name: Aisha
students.text: I prefer written messages. They leave a record, so nobody forgets what was agreed, and I can answer when it suits me instead of being interrupted.

students.name: Peter
students.text: For me, a short call is better. Long chains of messages can cause misunderstandings, and a five-minute conversation often solves a problem that would need twenty messages.

professor.name: Dr. Lopez
professor.text: Zoos say that they protect endangered species and teach people about wildlife. Animal rights groups argue that keeping wild animals in captivity is cruel, even in modern, well-designed zoos. As a society, should we continue to keep animals in zoos? Support your opinion with reasons.

students.name: Chloe
students.text: I think zoos still have an important role. Some species survive today only because zoos bred them, and children who see real animals learn to care about nature.

students.name: Ravi
students.text: I disagree. No enclosure can match the space animals have in the wild. We can learn about wildlife through documentaries and nature reserves without keeping animals captive.

professor.name: Professor Hughes
professor.text: E-books are cheaper and easier to carry than printed books, and many people now read mostly on screens. However, some readers say that paper books give a better reading experience and help them concentrate. Do you think printed books will eventually disappear, or will they remain important? Explain.

students.name: Mei
students.text: I think printed books will survive. Many people enjoy holding a book, and paper doesn't cause eye strain. They are also nice as gifts and for decoration.

students.name: Josh
students.text: In my opinion, e-books will win. You can store hundreds of books on one device, and you can change the text size. Most of my friends already read on their phones.

professor.name: Dr. Weiss
professor.text: The gig economy, in which people work through apps as drivers, delivery couriers, or freelancers, offers flexible schedules. At the same time, these workers often lack benefits such as health insurance or paid holidays. Do you think the gig economy is mostly good or mostly bad for workers? Give reasons.

students.name: Ana
students.text: For many people it is positive. Students and parents can choose their hours and earn money around other responsibilities, which a regular job rarely allows.

students.name: Brian
students.text: I see more problems than advantages. Without stable income or protection, a slow week or an injury can cause serious difficulty. Flexibility is not worth that risk.

professor.name: Professor Clarke
professor.text: More universities now offer complete degrees online. Online study is often cheaper and allows students to learn at any time and place. However, some people believe that attending classes in person gives a richer experience, with more contact with teachers and other students. Which kind of degree would you choose, and why?

students.name: Dina
students.text: I'd choose an online degree. I could keep a job, save money on housing, and study when I'm most alert. For many adults, it is the only realistic option.

students.name: Felix
students.text: I'd go to campus. Making friends, joining clubs, and talking with professors after class are a big part of university life, and a screen can't replace that.

professor.name: Dr. Harper
professor.text: Because information is now available on the internet, some people say that public libraries are no longer necessary and that the money would be better spent elsewhere. Library supporters say that libraries still serve important purposes in their communities. Do you think cities should continue to fund public libraries? Explain your opinion.

students.name: Olivia
students.text: Libraries are still essential. Not everyone has a computer or a quiet place to study, and libraries also offer programs for children, job seekers, and older people.

students.name: Mark
students.text: I think their role is shrinking. Most people now borrow digital books and search online, so cities could spend that money on services that more residents actually use.

professor.name: Professor Eriksen
professor.text: Some funding agencies now require scientists to make the data from their studies publicly available. Supporters argue that this improves transparency and allows other researchers to check and build on the results. Opponents are concerned about privacy, misuse of data, and the loss of the original researchers' effort. Should scientists be required to share their data openly?

students.name: Leila
students.text: I believe they should. Publicly funded research belongs to the public, and open data makes it much easier to detect errors and avoid repeating studies that have already been done.

students.name: Gabriel
students.text: There should be exceptions. Data about people can reveal identities even after names are removed, and researchers who collect data over years deserve first access to what they find.

professor.name: Dr. Andersson
professor.text: Several countries have experimented with universal basic income, a regular payment to every citizen regardless of their employment. Advocates claim that it would reduce poverty and give people the security to retrain or start businesses. Critics warn that it would be extremely expensive and might discourage people from working. Would you support such a policy? Use reasons and examples.

students.name: Camille
students.text: I would. Small pilot programs have shown that recipients usually keep working, and the security helps them make better long-term decisions about education, health, and housing.

students.name: Hassan
students.text: I have doubts. Paying every citizen is very costly, and the money would have to come from higher taxes or cuts elsewhere. Targeted support for people in need seems more efficient.

professor.name: Professor Tanaka
professor.text: English has become the dominant language of international science. Researchers whose first language is different must publish and present in English to be taken seriously. Some scholars see this as a practical way to share knowledge, while others believe it limits diversity of thought and disadvantages non-native speakers. How should the scientific community respond?

students.name: Sofia
students.text: A common language is extremely useful, because it lets scientists from every country collaborate easily. The cost of translation and misunderstanding would otherwise slow progress.

students.name: Dmitri
students.text: I think the situation is unfair. Brilliant researchers lose opportunities because of language, and valuable ideas published in other languages are overlooked. Journals should support translation and multilingual publication.

professor.name: Dr. Okafor
professor.text: Governments sometimes use small design changes, called nudges, to influence people's decisions without forbidding anything. For example, many countries automatically register citizens as organ donors unless they choose to opt out. Supporters say nudges are an effective and respectful way to improve public welfare. Critics argue that they are a form of manipulation. What is your view?

students.name: Rosa
students.text: I think nudges are acceptable when they are transparent and easy to reverse. People still have the freedom to choose, but the default helps those who would otherwise never get around to it.

students.name: Ethan
students.text: I'm uncomfortable with them. Even if no one is forced, officials decide what is best and design choices to get that outcome. Public debate and clear information are more honest.

professor.name: Professor Mbeki
professor.text: Cultural tourism brings money to communities that preserve traditional ways of life. Yet scholars have observed that when visitors arrive in large numbers, local customs can change in order to please tourists, and daily life may become a performance. Does tourism ultimately help or harm traditional cultures? Consider both sides in your answer.

students.name: Isla
students.text: It can help a great deal. Income from visitors gives communities a reason to keep crafts, music, and languages alive instead of abandoning them for work elsewhere.

students.name: Tariq
students.text: I think the damage is often underestimated. When customs are adjusted to meet the expectations of outsiders, they gradually lose their real meaning for the people who practice them.

professor.name: Dr. Lindgren
professor.text: Some instructors grade on a curve, so that a fixed percentage of students receive each grade. Others assign grades based on fixed standards, so that every student who reaches a certain level earns the same mark. Proponents of curves say they encourage competition and prevent grade inflation, while critics find them discouraging. Which approach do you consider more appropriate?

students.name: Nadia
students.text: I favor fixed standards. Grades should show what a student actually knows, not how others performed, and a curve can punish students for being in a strong class.

students.name: Oscar
students.text: A curve has its place in large courses. When exams differ in difficulty from year to year, it keeps grades comparable and prevents the marks from losing their meaning.

professor.name: Professor Bauer
professor.text: Social media platforms use algorithms to recommend content that keeps users engaged. Critics claim that these systems promote sensational or extreme material because it attracts attention. Companies respond that they only reflect what users want to see. To what extent should platforms be held responsible for the content their algorithms promote?

students.name: Yara
students.text: They should bear significant responsibility. Platforms design these systems and profit from them, so they cannot claim to be neutral when the design rewards outrage.

students.name: Henry
students.text: I'm wary of placing too much responsibility on companies. Users choose what to click, and strict rules could lead platforms to remove legitimate speech to avoid penalties.

professor.name: Dr. Petrova
professor.text: To reduce greenhouse gas emissions, governments can either tax carbon, making polluting activities more expensive, or introduce regulations that require certain technologies or limits. Economists often prefer taxes because they allow the market to find the cheapest solution, while others believe regulation is more predictable. Which policy do you think would be more effective?

students.name: Mateo
students.text: A carbon tax is more efficient. It gives every company a financial reason to cut emissions in whatever way is cheapest, and it avoids governments choosing specific technologies.

students.name: Freya
students.text: I'd favor regulation. Taxes can be absorbed by wealthy firms or passed on to consumers, while clear legal limits guarantee that emissions actually fall by a known amount.

professor.name: Professor Castellano
professor.text: Many governments spend public money on museums, orchestras, and theaters. Defenders argue that art enriches society and cannot survive on ticket sales alone. Critics say that public funds should go to essential services such as health and education, and that people who value art should pay for it. Should governments fund the arts?

students.name: Lucia
students.text: Yes. The arts shape a society's identity and create value that markets don't measure. Without support, only commercially successful work would survive, and culture would become poorer.

students.name: Nathan
students.text: I'm not convinced it's a priority. Resources are limited, and hospitals and schools have a more direct effect on people's lives. Private donors and audiences can support the arts.

professor.name: Dr. Mensah
professor.text: Some universities consider an applicant's socioeconomic background when making admissions decisions, taking into account the resources and challenges that the student faced. Supporters believe this makes admissions more equitable. Opponents argue that admissions should be based only on achievement and test results. Should universities consider an applicant's background? Support your position.

students.name: Alicia
students.text: They should. A good grade earned with little support is more impressive than the same grade earned with private tutors, so context tells admissions officers who has the most potential.

students.name: Robert
students.text: I disagree. Judging by background introduces subjective decisions and may feel unfair to individuals. Better funding for schools would address inequality at its source.
